subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Change Blindness
description: A quick, practical guide to Change Blindness.

hook.text: A stranger asks for directions. A door passes between you. The stranger changes. You don't notice.

buildup.text: Simons tested this with real people. 75% didn't notice the person they were talking to changed.

discovery.text: Change blindness: we fail to detect big changes when our attention is briefly interrupted.

twist.text: It's not about intelligence. Even trained observers miss changes during brief visual disruptions.

climax.text: Our brains build a rough sketch, not a photo. Any gap in attention lets changes slip through.

punchline.text: Seeing is believing, but we barely see.

quiz.question: When does change blindness typically occur?
options: When changes happen during an interruption
When objects are too small to see

details.summary: Change blindness is the failure to notice significant changes in a visual scene when the change occurs during a disruption like an eye movement, blink, or scene cut. It reveals that perception is far less detailed and continuous than we believe.
details.whyItMatters: Change blindness demonstrates that our sense of seeing everything is an illusion. We construct a perception of continuity from sparse samples. This has serious implications for eyewitness reliability and interface design.
takeaways: People fail to notice large changes when distracted during the transition
Our perception of continuous detailed awareness is a cognitive illusion
Change blindness undermines the reliability of eyewitness testimony

faq.question: What is the most famous change blindness experiment?
faq.answer: In the door study, a person asking directions was replaced by a completely different person during a brief interruption. Half the participants did not notice the swap. This revealed shockingly poor change detection even for the person you are talking to.

faq.question: How does change blindness affect real-world situations?
faq.answer: It undermines eyewitness testimony, makes drivers miss hazards that appear during saccades, and causes security officers to miss changes in surveillance footage. Any situation requiring change detection under disruption is vulnerable.
